title: Vertical Projectile Motion
seo_title: Grade 12 Physical Sciences: Vertical Projectile Motion Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 12 Physical Sciences: Vertical projectile motion in one dimension
standard_text: The motion of objects thrown vertically upwards or downwards, or dropped, near the Earth's surface; the acceleration is g = 9.8 m·s⁻² downwards; equations of motion; position–time, velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs for vertical projectile motion, including bouncing. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 12, Physics: Vertical projectile motion in one dimension)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): objects thrown up and dropped, free fall, equations of motion, and graphs of vertical motion. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The acceleration is always 9.8 m·s⁻² downwards.
key_sub: At the highest point v = 0, but a = g.
body_html:
How to think about it

A projectile moves under gravity alone (air resistance is ignored), so it is in free fall with a constant acceleration of 9,8 m·s⁻² downwards, whether it is moving up, at the top, or coming down. Choose up or down as positive and keep the signs consistent.

Use v = u + aΔt, Δy = uΔt + ½aΔt² and v² = u² + 2aΔy. The time to go up equals the time to come down to the same height. On a velocity–time graph the line is straight with a gradient of −9,8 m·s⁻² (up positive); the area gives the displacement.

Example

A ball is thrown up at 9,8 m·s⁻¹. Time to the top?

v = u + at

Answer: 1 s

Example

What is the acceleration at the highest point?

Gravity still acts.

Answer: 9,8 m·s⁻² downwards

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the acceleration is zero at the top.
  • Mixing up the signs of g and u.
  • Thinking a heavier ball falls faster when air resistance is ignored.

faq.q: What does the velocity–time graph of a bouncing ball look like?
faq.a: Straight sloping lines with the same gradient, with a sudden change of sign of the velocity at each bounce.

faq.q: Why does the ball take the same time to go up and come down?
faq.a: The acceleration is the same in both directions, so the motion is symmetrical.
